title: Is maths homework dead?
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton argues that free AI chatbots have destroyed the reliability of out-of-class maths homework as evidence of understanding. He opens with a friend's Year 8 daughter who now has ChatGPT complete her Sparx homework, and shows that a photo of a question, even a geometry one with an image, returns full working. From there he draws two consequences: students outsource the hard thinking, and teachers who rely on homework scores as a proxy for understanding are misled about who needs help. He weighs four responses (exhorting honesty, abolishing homework, making it optional, repurposing it) and rejects the first three as insufficient. His preferred fix is to make homework preparation for a paper-based in-class quiz, so that effort is held accountable where AI cannot be used. He admits the workload and curriculum-time costs but argues the quizzes double as retrieval practice.
points: Online homework platforms' anti-copying measures (personalised questions, written working) are now redundant because a phone photo gets a complete worked solution from a free chatbot.
Barton's demonstration that image-based geometry questions also fall to ChatGPT closes off the assumption that paper-based diagrammatic homework is safe.
The deeper harm is diagnostic: a student with full homework marks may know nothing, and the teacher never gives the help they need.
Making homework optional was tried at a school he visited, and the students who most needed practice were exactly those who skipped it.
His proposed solution reframes homework as preparation for a supervised in-class quiz, shifting accountability to a setting where AI use can be ruled out.
quotes: A fundamental problem with homework has always been that the teacher does not know the conditions under which it is completed, thus reducing its reliability as an assessment of understanding. Has the student done it all themselves, had help from a parent, or copied off the smart kid in the playground before school starts?

However, such measures are now redundant. Whether the homework is set online or paper-based, and regardless of the evidence of understanding that the teacher insists on seeing, today’s students all know where to go for all the help they need.

If the AI is doing all the hard thinking—what Peps Mccrea calls cognitive outsourcing—then students are unlikely to learn. Even those students who use AI as support, calling upon ChatGPT to help when they are stuck, may convince themselves that they understand when presented with the solution steps.

Because of AI, the reliability of homework for assessing student understanding has fallen off a cliff. A student who scores full marks in every homework may not have a clue what they are doing, and yet does not get the help they need from the teacher, who continues to rely on those scores as a proxy for that student’s understanding.
However, teachers cannot sanction students for not doing their homework. Can you predict what happened? Yep, the kids who most need to do homework are the very ones who choose not to do it.

One barrier to this solution is teacher workload—these quizzes need creating and marking. But that could be done centrally or solved by technology. Another barrier is time—every teacher will tell you the curriculum is too full, so they won’t have enough lesson time to dedicate to these regular quizzes.
